Ghostwriting and LinkedIn

Executive Ghostwriting That Builds Authority Fast

George Ukkuru|Co-founder, QualiPulse
Updated Jun 20, 2026|13 min read
On this page
  1. What Is Executive Ghostwriting
  2. Why Do Executives Use Ghostwriting
  3. How Does Executive Ghostwriting Actually Work
  4. What Content Formats Work Best For Executive Ghostwriting
  5. How Do You Find Quality Executive Ghostwriters
  6. What Does Executive Ghostwriting Cost
  7. When Should You Avoid Executive Ghostwriting
  8. How Do You Maintain Authenticity With Ghostwritten Content
  9. What Are Common Mistakes With Executive Ghostwriting
  10. How Does Executive Ghostwriting Fit With Content Strategy
  11. What Results Should You Expect From Executive Ghostwriting
  12. Frequently Asked Questions
  13. Making Executive Ghostwriting Work

Most executives understand that thought leadership matters. They see competitors publishing weekly. They watch peers build LinkedIn followings that turn into speaking gigs and board seats. They know visibility drives opportunity.

Then they look at their calendars. Board meetings. Investor calls. Team reviews. Strategic planning sessions. Customer meetings. The hours needed to write consistent, quality content simply do not exist.

Executive ghostwriting solves this exact problem. It allows busy leaders to maintain thought leadership without spending hours each week writing. Someone else handles drafting. You provide insights and direction. Your voice stays consistent. Your visibility keeps growing.

This guide explains how executive ghostwriting works, when it makes sense, and what separates effective ghostwriting from content that damages credibility.

What Is Executive Ghostwriting

Executive ghostwriting means hiring professional writers to create content published under your name. The ghostwriter interviews you, studies your communication style, and produces articles, LinkedIn posts, speeches, or books that sound like you wrote them.

This differs from standard content marketing. Generic company blog posts can be written by anyone with subject knowledge. Executive ghostwriting requires capturing your specific voice, perspectives, and experiences. The content needs to reflect how you actually think and communicate.

The practice spans multiple formats. Some executives use ghostwriters for LinkedIn posts. Others commission full books. Many do both, plus keynote speeches, industry articles, and internal communications. The common thread is professional content production that maintains your voice without requiring your writing time.

Why Do Executives Use Ghostwriting

Time constraints drive most executive ghostwriting decisions. Writing well takes longer than most people expect. A thoughtful 1000-word article requires research, drafting, editing, and revision. That process easily consumes four to six hours.

Executives have insights worth sharing, but limited bandwidth to share them. They understand market dynamics, strategic thinking, and leadership challenges. They cannot spend ten hours weekly turning those insights into publishable content.

Executive ghostwriting also addresses skill gaps. Not every strong leader writes compelling content. Some struggle with structure. Others cannot translate spoken thoughts into readable prose. Ghostwriters bridge that gap without forcing executives to become professional writers.

The Professional Visibility Problem

Executive visibility now demands consistent content. Boards want leaders with industry presence. Investors check thought leadership before meetings. Customers research executives before signing contracts. Silence creates doubt about expertise.

But publishing inconsistently damages credibility as much as not publishing. Three great articles followed by six months of silence signal that the initial content came from a PR push, not genuine expertise. Executive ghostwriting maintains the consistency professional visibility requires. Learn more about personal brand ghostwriting strategies that help leaders stay visible without overwhelming their schedules.

How Does Executive Ghostwriting Actually Work

Effective executive ghostwriting starts with voice calibration. The ghostwriter studies how you communicate. They read past emails, watch recorded presentations, and review previous articles. They identify your vocabulary, sentence structure, and thinking patterns.

Then comes the interview phase. You discuss the topic for 30 to 45 minutes. The ghostwriter asks targeted questions to extract your specific insights. They dig past surface observations to find perspectives only you can provide.

After the interview, the ghostwriter drafts content in your voice. First drafts typically capture 70 to 80 percent of your style. You provide feedback on what sounds right and what needs adjustment. This revision cycle continues until the content authentically represents how you think and communicate.

The Interview Process

Good ghostwriters ask questions that surface original insights. They avoid generic prompts like “tell me about leadership.” Instead, they ask about specific decisions, challenges faced, and tradeoffs made. These details separate authentic expertise from recycled business clichés.

The best interviews feel conversational, not interrogative. You talk through ideas the same way you would with colleagues. The ghostwriter guides the discussion toward useful material without making it feel scripted.

What Content Formats Work Best For Executive Ghostwriting

Different formats serve different executive visibility goals. The right choice depends on your industry, audience, and where you need presence.

LinkedIn Posts and Articles

LinkedIn remains the primary platform for executive visibility in 2026. Regular posting keeps you visible to your network and attracts connections outside it. For executives building professional LinkedIn presence, ghostwritten content maintains consistent visibility without demanding excessive time investment.

Ghostwritten LinkedIn content typically includes short posts, weekly updates, and longer articles. Posts generate engagement. Articles demonstrate depth. Together, they position you as an active thought leader in your space.

Books and Long-Form Thought Leadership

Books remain the ultimate credibility signal. A published book opens doors to speaking engagements, media interviews, and consulting opportunities that LinkedIn posts cannot match.

Writing a book takes most people 12 to 18 months. Executive ghostwriting compresses that timeline to 4 to 6 months while maintaining quality. You provide expertise through structured interviews. The ghostwriter handles research, organization, and prose.

Keynote Speeches and Presentations

Speaking opportunities arrive when executive visibility reaches critical mass. But creating compelling presentations requires different skills from running a company.

Ghostwriters craft speech content that translates your expertise into audience value. They structure narratives, develop examples, and write for spoken delivery rather than written consumption.

Internal Communications

Executive communications to employees require a different tone than external content. Internal ghostwriting helps leaders communicate vision, change, and direction clearly to teams.

Town hall scripts, company-wide emails, and strategic announcements all benefit from ghostwriting. Clear internal communication builds trust and alignment across organizations.

How Do You Find Quality Executive Ghostwriters

Not all ghostwriters can handle executive content. The skill set differs from general content writing. You need someone who can interview well, capture voice accurately, and produce content that passes as authentically yours.

Look For Interviewing Skills

Great executive ghostwriters extract insights through conversation. They ask follow-up questions that dig deeper. They recognize when an answer contains the seed of something valuable and explore it.

During initial conversations, notice whether potential ghostwriters listen actively or wait to talk. The best ones guide discussions without dominating them. They make you feel heard while keeping the conversation productive.

Review Voice Matching Samples

Ask for examples where the ghostwriter matched different client voices. Read samples aloud. Do they sound like distinct people or do they all sound like the same writer with minor vocabulary changes?

Voice matching ability separates executive ghostwriters from general content creators. Some writers produce clean, professional prose that lacks individual personality. That works fine for corporate blogs. It fails for executive visibility. For leaders needing content that builds authentic authority, QualiPulse provides ghostwriters who capture executive voice while maintaining technical credibility.

Check Industry Familiarity

Ghostwriters do not need deep expertise in your field. But they should understand your industry well enough to ask intelligent questions and recognize relevant insights when you share them.

Someone who has written for software executives understands SaaS business models, product development cycles, and technical team dynamics. They catch nuance a generalist would miss. This familiarity makes interviews more productive and reduces revision cycles.

What Does Executive Ghostwriting Cost

Pricing varies dramatically based on deliverable type, ghostwriter experience, and time commitment required.

LinkedIn Content Pricing

Monthly LinkedIn ghostwriting typically runs $1500 to $5000. This usually includes 4 to 8 posts plus one longer article. Premium ghostwriters charge the high end. Newer writers or overseas talent charge less.

The investment makes sense when you calculate opportunity cost. If six hours monthly writing content prevents you from closing one additional deal or securing one board seat, ghostwriting pays for itself immediately.

Book Ghostwriting Fees

Full book ghostwriting ranges from $30,000 to $150,000 for business books. Executive memoirs and high-profile projects command higher fees. The wide range reflects ghostwriter experience, book complexity, and time investment required.

Lower-priced options exist but often produce generic content. A $15,000 book typically comes from junior writers or overseas services. The prose reads cleanly but lacks the voice specificity executive brands require.

Speech Writing Costs

Keynote speeches range from $2,000 to $10,000, depending on length and complexity. A 20-minute keynote typically costs $3,000 to $5,000. Longer presentations or those requiring extensive research cost more.

When Should You Avoid Executive Ghostwriting

Ghostwriting works brilliantly for many executives. But some situations call for personally written content or no content at all.

When You Enjoy Writing

Some leaders find writing clarifies their thinking. The act of organizing ideas into prose helps them process complex problems. If writing serves this function for you, ghostwriting removes a valuable thinking tool.

However, you can split the difference. Write pieces that help you think. Hire ghostwriters for content that maintains visibility but does not require deep reflection.

When Your Industry Values Authenticity Signals

Certain fields prize rough, unpolished communication as proof of authenticity. Startup founders often write with intentional informality. Over-polished content signals they have hired PR teams, which damages the scrappy founder persona.

In these cases, light editing works better than full ghostwriting. Write your own drafts. Have someone clean up grammar and structure without changing your voice.

How Do You Maintain Authenticity With Ghostwritten Content

The biggest concern about executive ghostwriting is authenticity. If someone else writes your content, does it still represent you?

The answer depends entirely on process quality. Good ghostwriting captures and amplifies your actual thinking. Poor ghostwriting generates generic content with your name attached.

Your Ideas Must Drive The Content

Authentic executive ghostwriting starts with your insights. The ghostwriter cannot invent your perspectives. They can only shape and present ideas you actually hold.

This means you invest time in interviews and review cycles. Ghostwriting saves you from drafting and editing. It does not eliminate your involvement. Content quality directly correlates with how much genuine insight you provide. For executives seeking ghostwriting that preserves authentic voice, working with experienced practitioners ensures content reflects genuine expertise rather than researched platitudes.

Voice Consistency Matters More Than Perfection

Your ghostwritten content should sound consistently like you across all platforms. Minor imperfections that match your natural communication style signal authenticity more than overly polished prose.

If you occasionally use sentence fragments in conversation, ghostwritten content can include them. If you favor certain phrases or examples, those should appear in written content. Perfect grammar matters less than sounding like yourself.

What Are Common Mistakes With Executive Ghostwriting

Most ghostwriting failures follow predictable patterns. Recognizing these helps you avoid wasting time and money on content that damages rather than builds your brand.

Skipping The Voice Calibration Phase

Some executives hire ghostwriters and immediately request content. They skip the voice study phase because it feels inefficient. This saves two weeks upfront and costs months in revision cycles.

Without voice calibration, ghostwriters produce generic executive content. It reads professionally but sounds nothing like you. Your audience notices. The content generates views but builds no authentic connection.

Publishing Without Reviewing

Executive ghostwriting requires your review before publication. You cannot outsource both creation and approval. The moment something is published under your name, you own every claim, every opinion, every factual assertion.

Reading drafts takes time, but far less than writing from scratch. This review also improves future content. Your feedback teaches ghostwriters what works and what needs adjustment.

Hiring Based Only On Price

Ghostwriting costs reflect writer’s quality. The cheapest option rarely delivers content worth publishing. Budget ghostwriters produce grammatically correct articles that lack distinctive voice or original insight.

This creates a worse outcome than no content. Generic ghostwritten material positioned as your thought leadership damages credibility. Readers recognize content that could apply to anyone in your industry. They stop trusting your brand.

How Does Executive Ghostwriting Fit With Content Strategy

Executive ghostwriting works best as part of a broader content strategy. The ghostwritten pieces should align with business goals and complement other brand-building activities.

Define what you want executive visibility to accomplish. More speaking invitations? Board positions? Client acquisition? Talent recruitment? Each goal suggests different content priorities and platforms.

Your ghostwriter should understand these goals. The content they produce should move you toward specific outcomes, not just generate activity for its own sake.

Coordinating Across Platforms

Executive brands exist across multiple channels. LinkedIn, company blog, conference talks, podcast appearances. Ghostwritten content should reinforce consistent themes rather than introducing disconnected ideas.

This requires planning content calendars beyond individual posts. What topics position you as the expert you want to be known as? What perspectives differentiate you from your peers? These strategic questions guide what ghostwriters should produce.

What Results Should You Expect From Executive Ghostwriting

Executive ghostwriting produces measurable outcomes when executed well. But timeline and specific results vary based on your industry, existing visibility, and content quality.

Early Stage Results

The first three months establish consistency. Your audience notices regular publishing. Engagement typically remains modest. You are building habit and credibility, not virality.

During this phase, focus on voice refinement over reach. Work with your ghostwriter to nail how the content should sound. This foundation determines all future quality.

Medium Term Growth

After six months of consistent ghostwritten content, your network expands. Connection requests increase. Speaking invitations arrive. Media outlets reach out for expert commentary.

These opportunities compound. One keynote leads to podcast interviews. Podcast appearances generate LinkedIn followers. Followers become clients or partners. Content creates a visibility flywheel that accelerates over time.

Long Term Brand Equity

After 12 to 18 months, executive visibility becomes a business asset. Clients mention your content during sales calls. Recruiters cite your thought leadership when pitching candidates. Board searches include you because your expertise is publicly visible.

This brand equity persists beyond individual pieces. Even if you pause content production, established authority remains. The ghostwritten library continues attracting opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is executive ghostwriting?

Executive ghostwriting means hiring professional writers to create content published under your name. The ghostwriter interviews you to understand your perspectives, then produces articles, posts, speeches, or books that sound like you wrote them. This allows busy executives to maintain thought leadership without spending hours writing each week while preserving authentic voice and strategic messaging.

Is executive ghostwriting ethical?

Yes, when done properly. Ghostwriting is ethical if the ideas come from you and the content accurately represents your thinking. The ghostwriter provides writing skills, not expertise. This differs from plagiarism or false attribution. Most executives, politicians, and public figures use ghostwriters for speeches and articles. The practice is standard in professional communication and widely accepted.

How much does executive ghostwriting cost?

Monthly LinkedIn ghostwriting typically costs $1500 to $5000 for posts and articles. Full book ghostwriting ranges from $30,000 to $150,000, depending on complexity and ghostwriter experience. Keynote speeches cost $2,000 to $10,000. Pricing reflects time investment for interviews, research, writing, and revisions. Premium ghostwriters charge higher rates but deliver better voice matching and insight extraction.

How do you find a good executive ghostwriter?

Look for ghostwriters with strong interviewing skills and proven voice-matching ability. Review samples from different clients to verify they sound distinct. Ask about their process for understanding your communication style. Check whether they have industry familiarity relevant to your work. The best ghostwriters make interviews feel conversational while extracting specific insights that separate your content from generic business writing.

How long does executive ghostwriting take?

Initial setup, including voice calibration, takes 2 to 4 weeks. After that, individual LinkedIn posts require 30-minute interviews and 3 to 5 days for drafting. Longer articles need 45 to 60-minute interviews and 1 to 2 weeks of production time. Books take 4 to 6 months from the first interview to the completed manuscript. Your time investment averages 2 to 4 hours monthly for ongoing content.

Can ghostwriters match your executive voice accurately?

Skilled ghostwriters can match voices very accurately after proper calibration. They study your past writing, watch recorded talks, and conduct detailed interviews about communication preferences. First drafts typically capture 70 to 80 percent of your voice. Revision cycles refine accuracy until the content sounds authentically like you. Voice matching is a learnable skill that improves as ghostwriters understand your thinking better.

What content formats work for executive ghostwriting?

Common formats include LinkedIn posts and articles, keynote speeches, business books, thought leadership pieces, internal communications, and conference presentations. Different formats serve different goals. LinkedIn builds ongoing visibility. Books establish ultimate credibility. Speeches extend reach beyond written channels. Most successful executives use multiple ghostwritten formats coordinated around consistent themes and strategic messaging priorities.

Do you need to review ghostwritten content before publishing?

Yes, always review content before it is published under your name. You own every claim and opinion once it goes live. Reviewing also improves future quality by teaching ghostwriters what works. The review takes far less time than writing from scratch. Budget 15 to 30 minutes per piece for feedback. Skip this step, and you risk publishing content that misrepresents your views or contains errors.

When should you avoid using executive ghostwriters?

Avoid ghostwriting if you genuinely enjoy writing, and it helps you think. Also, skip it if your industry values rough, unpolished communication as an authenticity signals. In these cases, write your own content or hire light editors instead of full ghostwriters. Ghostwriting works best when time constraints prevent you from writing, but visibility demands consistent content publication.

How quickly do you see results from ghostwritten executive content?

Initial results appear within 60 to 90 days as publishing consistency becomes visible. Meaningful business impact typically takes 6 months as your network expands and opportunities compound. After 12 to 18 months, executive visibility becomes a significant business asset, generating speaking invitations, media requests, and client interest. Timeline varies based on existing visibility and content quality consistency.

Making Executive Ghostwriting Work

Executive ghostwriting works when you bring genuine insights and hire skilled writers to shape them. It fails when you outsource both thinking and writing, producing generic content with your name attached.

The decision to use ghostwriters is not about whether you can write. Many executives write well. It is about whether writing is the best use of your limited hours. If publishing consistent thought leadership matters to your career but you cannot spare ten hours weekly to produce it, ghostwriting solves a real problem.

The key is finding ghostwriters who genuinely capture your voice and extract your specific insights. Generic business content damages your brand regardless of how polished it reads. Content that sounds authentically like you builds credibility that compounds over time.

Invest time in the interview and review process. Your involvement determines content quality. Ghostwriting saves you from drafting and editing, not from thinking and approving. Done well, it gives you the executive visibility your expertise deserves without burning the hours you need for actual leadership.

How to Find Ghostwriters: A Buying Guide for Software Companies

George Ukkuru|Co-founder, QualiPulse
Updated May 11, 2026|12 min read
On this page
  1. Where Do You Find Ghostwriters?
  2. How Do You Screen Ghostwriters for Software Knowledge?
  3. What Questions Should You Ask When Interviewing Ghostwriters?
  4. How Much Should You Pay Ghostwriters?
  5. What Are Red Flags When Hiring Ghostwriters?
  6. How Should You Run a Trial Project with Ghostwriters?
  7. What Should You Ask Ghostwriter References?
  8. How QualiPulse Solves the Ghostwriter Search Problem
  9. Frequently Asked Questions About Finding Ghostwriters
  10. Final Thoughts on Finding Ghostwriters

You posted a job listing for a content writer. You got 47 applications. Three applicants have software experience. Two of those charge $2,000 per post. The third has never written a blog before.

Finding ghostwriters who can write technical content is harder than most software companies expect. The good writers are already booked. The available writers don’t understand your product. The writers who claim software expertise Googled your industry yesterday.

This guide shows you how to find ghostwriters who actually know software, how to screen for technical credibility, what to pay, and where technical writers hang out. These aren’t generic hiring tips. This is the vetting process that separates practitioners from people who write landing pages for SaaS companies they’ve never used.

The challenge isn’t finding writers. Thousands of freelancers call themselves ghostwriters. The challenge is finding writers who can explain API architecture, compare deployment strategies, and write case studies that technical buyers actually believe.

Where Do You Find Ghostwriters?

Ghostwriters cluster in specific places based on their specialization. Knowing where to look saves time and improves the quality of candidates you screen.

Industry-Specific Communities

Technical ghostwriters hang out in developer communities, not generic freelance marketplaces. Check communities like Write the Docs, Dev.to, Hacker News freelancer threads, and software testing communities. Writers in these spaces understand technical concepts because they participate in technical discussions.

LinkedIn works for finding ghostwriters if you search correctly. Don’t search for a content writer. Search for a QA engineer writer, a developer advocate writer, or a technical program manager writer. You want people who moved from technical roles into writing, not people who write about technical topics.

Freelance Platforms

Upwork and Fiverr have thousands of ghostwriters. Most are generalists. Filter aggressively. Search for ghostwriters who list software tools in their profiles. Check if they have developer or QA certifications. Read their portfolio descriptions to see if they understand what they wrote about or just rewrote competitor content.

Toptal and similar vetted platforms claim to screen for quality. The vetting process checks writing skills, not domain knowledge. You still need to verify the software background yourself.

Referrals from Other Software Companies

Ask other software companies who writes their content. Most are happy to share ghostwriter contacts if they had good experiences. Referrals come pre-screened for technical accuracy and reliability.

Check the content you admire. If a competitor publishes great technical blog posts, find out who writes them. Many ghostwriters list client work in portfolios or LinkedIn profiles.

Content Agencies vs Independent Ghostwriters

Content agencies provide account management and multi-channel distribution, but charge premium prices. Independent ghostwriters cost less and often specialize more deeply. Agencies make sense if you need turnkey content operations. Independent writers make sense if you can manage strategy internally.

How Do You Screen Ghostwriters for Software Knowledge?

Screening separates ghostwriters who understand software from ghostwriters who claim they can write about anything. Use these tests before you waste time on interviews.

Check Portfolio for Technical Depth

Ask for three software writing samples. Read them critically. Do the posts explain how things work or just what they do? Do the examples feel real or generic? Does the writer use technical terminology correctly?

Good technical writing includes specific details. Bad technical writing stays at the concept level. If every sample could have been written by someone who spent 20 minutes on your competitor’s website, the ghostwriter lacks depth.

Ask About Their Technical Background

Ask directly what software roles they’ve held. Have they worked as a developer, QA engineer, product manager, or DevOps specialist? How long? What technologies did they work with?

Writers who transitioned from technical roles bring domain knowledge that generalists can’t fake. They know which concepts need explanation and which are common knowledge among your audience.

Test Their Research Process

Ask how they handle topics they don’t fully understand. Good ghostwriters describe a research process: reading documentation, testing product features, interviewing SMEs, and verifying technical claims. Bad ghostwriters say they Google it and figure it out.

Give them a mini assignment. Pick a feature from your product and ask them to explain how they’d research it for a blog post. Their answer reveals whether they know how to extract information from technical sources.

Check for AI Reliance

Ask directly whether they use AI tools. Some ghostwriters use ChatGPT for first drafts, then edit heavily. Others write entirely by hand. AI-generated content lacks specificity and uses predictable patterns.

Request a sample that you run through AI detection tools. If it flags as AI-generated and the ghostwriter claimed human writing, they’re lying. If they’re honest about AI usage, decide whether that’s acceptable for your content standards.

What Questions Should You Ask When Interviewing Ghostwriters?

These interview questions reveal whether a ghostwriter can handle software content or just claims they can.

Have you worked in software roles before becoming a writer?

This question establishes domain credibility. Writers who spent years in QA, development, or product roles understand software differently than writers who only write about it. Ask follow-up questions about what they built, what problems they solved, and what technologies they used.

What software companies have you written for?

Past client experience in your industry matters. A ghostwriter who has written for testing tools, DevOps platforms, or developer tools brings relevant context. Ask for client references you can contact.

How do you handle topics you don’t understand?

This reveals their research process. Good answers include reading documentation, testing features, interviewing engineers, and admitting knowledge gaps. Bad answers involve Googling and winging it.

What’s your typical turnaround time for a technical blog post?

Realistic timelines matter. A ghostwriter who promises a 2,000-word technical post in 24 hours is cutting corners. Quality technical content takes time for research, writing, and internal review. Expect one to two weeks for complex posts.

How do you capture company voice?

Voice capture separates good ghostwriters from mediocre ones. Good answers describe interviewing team members, reviewing existing content, and iterating based on feedback. Bad answers claim they can match any voice after reading your website.

How Much Should You Pay Ghostwriters?

Ghostwriter pricing varies by expertise, deliverable type, and engagement model. Here’s what software companies actually pay.

Per-Post Pricing

Technical blog posts cost $500 to $1,500, depending on complexity and research requirements. Simple how-to guides land at the low end. Deep technical analyses requiring product testing and SME interviews land at the high end.

LinkedIn ghostwriting costs $500 to $1,200 per month for weekly posts. LinkedIn ghostwriters maintain consistent posting schedules and handle engagement monitoring.

Case studies cost $800 to $2,000 per piece. Pricing depends on whether the ghostwriter conducts customer interviews or works from information you provide.

Monthly Retainer Pricing

Monthly retainers for ongoing blog ghostwriting range from $2,000 to $6,000. Most software companies get two to four blog posts per month at this price point.

Content agencies charge $5,000 to $15,000 monthly because they bundle strategy, SEO, and distribution with writing. You’re paying for account management and reporting infrastructure.

Budget vs Premium Pricing

Budget ghostwriters on Upwork or Fiverr charge $100 to $300 per post. The quality reflects the price. These writers lack software background and produce generic content that damages credibility.

Premium ghostwriters charge $1,500+ per post. You’re paying for deep expertise, minimal hand-holding, and content that technical readers actually respect. The premium makes sense when credibility matters more than cost.

What Are Red Flags When Hiring Ghostwriters?

These warning signs indicate a ghostwriter will waste your time or produce low-quality content.

No Software Portfolio Samples

If a ghostwriter claims software expertise but can’t show technical writing samples, they’re learning on your budget. Insist on seeing three relevant samples before scheduling interviews.

Claims They Can Write About Anything

Generalist ghostwriters who write about healthcare, finance, and software equally well are surface-level writers. Technical content requires domain knowledge. Writers who specialize produce better work than writers who claim universal expertise.

Promises Unrealistic Turnaround Times

A ghostwriter who promises a 2,000-word technical post in 48 hours is cutting corners. Quality content takes time for research, writing, and internal review. Fast turnarounds mean shallow research or AI-generated drafts.

Vague About Their Process

When asked about research methods, voice capture, or revision processes, vague answers indicate lack of a systematic approach. Good ghostwriters describe specific steps. Bad ghostwriters give generic answers about doing whatever it takes.

Won’t Commit to Human-Written Content

If a ghostwriter gives evasive answers about AI usage or says AI is just a tool they use for ideation, they’re probably using ChatGPT more than they admit. Writers confident in their work commit to human writing without hedging.

How Should You Run a Trial Project with Ghostwriters?

Trial projects reveal whether a ghostwriter can actually deliver what they promised in the interview. Structure trials carefully to test the right capabilities.

Pick a Real Topic, Not a Test Assignment

Choose a blog topic you actually need written. This tests whether the ghostwriter produces usable content, not whether they can complete an exercise. You’ll publish good trial posts and learn from bad ones without wasting the work.

Provide Context but Not Excessive Hand-Holding

Share your target audience, key points to cover, and any required resources like documentation links. Don’t write an outline for them. You’re testing whether they can structure content independently.

Set Clear Deliverable Expectations

Specify word count, deadline, and revision policy upfront. Make it clear this is a paid trial, not spec work. Professional ghostwriters won’t work for free on trial projects.

Evaluate Technical Accuracy First

Have your engineering team review the trial post for technical errors before evaluating the writing style. A well-written post with technical mistakes is worse than useful content that needs polish. Technical accuracy is non-negotiable. Voice is fixable.

Test Revision Responsiveness

Request one round of revisions even if the trial post is good. You’re testing how the ghostwriter handles feedback. Do they get defensive? Do they implement changes accurately? Do they ask clarifying questions? Revision dynamics matter as much as initial quality.

What Should You Ask Ghostwriter References?

References reveal reliability and working dynamics that portfolios don’t show. Ask specific questions that surface actual problems.

How much technical hand-holding did the ghostwriter need?

This question reveals whether the ghostwriter required constant engineering team input or researched independently. Ghostwriters who need extensive technical explanations for every post slow down your team.

Did they miss deadlines or communicate delays proactively?

Reliability matters for content calendars. Missing deadlines without warning breaks publishing schedules. Ghostwriters who communicate delays early let you adjust plans.

How many revision rounds did posts typically need?

Excessive revisions indicate the ghostwriter didn’t understand the requirements or struggled with voice capture. One to two revision rounds are normal. Five rounds per post signal problems.

What did your engineering team think of the technical accuracy?

This cuts through marketing-speak and gets technical validation. If the reference says their engineers caught lots of errors, the ghostwriter lacks domain knowledge.

How QualiPulse Solves the Ghostwriter Search Problem

Finding ghostwriters who understand software takes weeks of screening. Most software companies don’t have time to interview 20 candidates, run trial projects, and check references.

QualiPulse skips the search process entirely. Our ghostwriters have built enterprise software, run QA programs, and spoken at industry conferences. They understand technical concepts without needing your engineering team to explain everything.

We offer two services. Blog content from $460 per month includes four articles written and reviewed by practitioners. LinkedIn ghostwriting from $400 per month covers 8 posts, about two a week, for software executives. No contracts. No setup fees.

The difference between QualiPulse and hiring random ghostwriters is technical credibility. We’ve shipped software. We understand testing frameworks, deployment pipelines, and API design. We write content that technical readers respect.

If you want to vet ghostwriters yourself, use this guide. If you want to skip the search and get started immediately, we’re already here.

Frequently Asked Questions About Finding Ghostwriters

Where is the best place to find ghostwriters for software content?

The best places to find ghostwriters with software expertise are industry communities like Write the Docs, developer forums, and LinkedIn searches for technical roles combined with writer. Referrals from other software companies work well because they come pre-screened for technical accuracy. General freelance platforms like Upwork have thousands of ghostwriters but require aggressive filtering to find specialists. Avoid generalist content marketplaces unless you have time to screen dozens of candidates.

How do you know if a ghostwriter actually understands software?

Check their work history for technical roles like QA engineer, developer, DevOps specialist, or technical program manager. Review portfolio samples for technical depth and accurate terminology. Ask them to explain their research process for unfamiliar topics. Run a paid trial project and have your engineering team review for technical errors. Ghostwriters who’ve worked in software understand concepts differently than writers who only write about software.

Should you hire freelance ghostwriters or content agencies?

Hire freelance ghostwriters if you can manage content strategy and publishing workflows internally. They cost less and often specialize more deeply than agency writers. Hire content agencies if you need turnkey operations, including strategy, distribution, and reporting. Agencies charge premium prices but reduce coordination burden. Most software companies start with freelance specialists and switch to agencies only when volume scales beyond what one writer handles.

How much should you pay ghostwriters for software content?

Technical blog posts cost $500 to $1,500 per post, depending on complexity. Monthly retainers for ongoing ghostwriting range from $2,000 to $6,000 for two to four posts per month. Content agencies charge $5,000 to $15,000 monthly, including strategy and distribution. Budget writers on Upwork charge $100 to $300 but lack software expertise. Premium ghostwriters charge $1,500+ per post but produce content that technical readers respect. Pay reflects expertise and reliability.

What questions should you ask when interviewing ghostwriters?

Ask about previous software roles they’ve held. Ask which software companies they’ve written for and request client references. Ask how they handle topics they don’t understand to test their research process. Ask about typical turnaround times for technical posts to check if they’re realistic. Ask how they capture the company voice to see if they have a systematic approach. These questions separate ghostwriters who understand software from ghostwriters who claim universal expertise.

What are red flags when hiring ghostwriters?

Red flags include no software portfolio samples, claims they can write about any industry equally well, promises of unrealistic turnaround times like 2,000 words in 48 hours, vague answers about research or revision processes, and unwillingness to commit to human-written content. These signals indicate the ghostwriter lacks specialization, cuts corners, or relies heavily on AI tools. Professional ghostwriters with software expertise have clear processes and realistic timelines.

Should you run trial projects before hiring ghostwriters?

Yes, always run paid trial projects before committing to monthly retainers. Pick a real topic you need written, not a test assignment. Provide context but don’t hand-hold excessively. Have your engineering team review for technical accuracy first. Test how the ghostwriter handles revision feedback. Trial projects reveal reliability, technical knowledge, and working dynamics that interviews and portfolios don’t show. Budget one to two weeks for trial completion and review.

How long does it take to find good ghostwriters?

Finding ghostwriters with software expertise typically takes three to six weeks. Plan one week for posting job listings and collecting applications. Two weeks for screening portfolios and conducting interviews. One to two weeks for running trial projects and checking references. Budget more time if you’re searching through general freelance platforms, where most candidates lack a software background. Referrals from other software companies can shorten the timeline significantly.

Final Thoughts on Finding Ghostwriters

Finding ghostwriters who understand software is harder than finding writers who claim they can write about anything. The good ones are already booked. The available ones lack a technical background. The cheap ones produce content that makes your company look less technical than it actually is.

The search process takes weeks. You’ll screen dozens of portfolios. You’ll interview candidates who sound great but can’t deliver. You’ll run trial projects that reveal technical gaps. You’ll check references that tell you what you should have asked earlier.

How to Hire a QA Content Writer That Drives Pipeline

George Ukkuru|Co-founder, QualiPulse
Updated Sep 19, 2026|17 min read
On this page
  1. What Is a QA Content Writer and Why Is This Role Harder to Fill Than It Looks?
  2. What Should You Actually Look for When You Hire a QA Content Writer?
  3. What Are the Biggest Mistakes Testing Companies Make When They Hire a Content Writer?
  4. Freelancer, In-House, or Specialist Partner: Which Model Works for Testing Companies?
  5. How Do You Run a Hiring Process That Actually Identifies the Right QA Content Writer?
  6. Why Working with a Specialist QA Content Partner Is Often the Better Alternative
  7. Frequently Asked Questions on How to Hire a QA Content Writer?
  8. Conclusion

If you have ever typed hire a QA content writer into a search engine, you already know what comes back: platforms full of QA engineers available for testing contracts. That is not what you need. What you need is a writer who understands the software testing industry well enough to produce content that your actual buyers, QA directors, engineering managers, and CTOs at software companies, will read and trust. Those are two completely different people, and the confusion between them costs testing companies real money.

Most testing companies that set out to hire a content writer end up with one of two bad outcomes. They hire a generalist who researches QA topics and produces technically hollow content that fails to earn credibility with a practitioner audience. Or they hire someone with testing knowledge who cannot write in a way that works for search, for buyers, or for the long-form formats that content marketing requires. The sweet spot between those two failure modes is narrow, and it is worth understanding exactly what it looks like before you start the search.

This article gives you a clear picture of what a qualified QA content writer actually is, what to look for when you hire one, what the common mistakes are in the hiring process, and why the model you choose, freelancer, in-house hire, or specialist partner, matters more than most companies realize before they have already made the wrong call.

What Is a QA Content Writer and Why Is This Role Harder to Fill Than It Looks?

A QA content writer produces long-form articles, whitepapers, guides, and thought leadership pieces specifically for the software testing industry. The role sits at the intersection of two disciplines that rarely overlap cleanly: genuine practitioner knowledge of quality assurance, and professional content writing with SEO fluency and an understanding of B2B buyer psychology.

Most content writers are good at one of those two things. The ones who are technically strong tend to write in ways that feel like internal documentation rather than content designed to attract and convert buyers. The ones who are strong on structure and SEO tend to produce content that is technically shallow in ways that QA practitioners spot immediately. Finding someone who holds both skills at a level that serves a demanding technical audience is the actual challenge.

Why the Practitioner Test Matters More in QA Than in Most Niches

QA engineers and test managers are trained skeptics. That is part of the job. They read content with the same critical mindset they bring to reviewing test plans or evaluating a new automation framework. If an article about test coverage strategy does not reflect the reality of how coverage decisions actually get made under delivery pressure, they know. If a piece about shift-left testing does not acknowledge the organizational friction that comes with it, they recognize the gap immediately.

This means a QA content writer who learned about testing through research rather than experience will produce content that ranks but does not convert. The traffic comes. The practitioner reader arrives, reads two paragraphs, and leaves. That pattern is invisible in standard analytics but it explains why so many testing companies publish consistently and see zero inbound from their content investment.

Quick Definition: What Is a QA Content Writer?

A QA content writer is a specialist who creates marketing content for software testing companies, QA tool vendors, and testing consultancies. Unlike a general technical writer, their focus is on content that attracts buyers, earns search rankings, and builds brand authority in the QA space. The role requires both practitioner-level understanding of testing concepts and professional-grade content writing skills.

What Should You Actually Look for When You Hire a QA Content Writer?

The hiring criteria for a QA content writer should be different from the criteria you would apply to hiring a general content writer. Here is what the evaluation actually needs to cover.

Criterion One: The Practitioner Test

The single most important filter when you hire a QA content writer is whether their sample work passes the practitioner test. Take one of their portfolio pieces on a testing topic and show it to a working QA engineer or test lead on your team without telling them who wrote it. Ask them whether it reads like it was written by someone who has done the work or by someone who researched it. That feedback is more reliable than any job description, credential or agency pitch.

Specific things the practitioner test reveals: Does the writer understand the difference between coverage as a metric and coverage as a risk management decision? Can they explain why automation suites degrade over time without using a definition they clearly read from a glossary? Do they take positions on contested testing questions, or do they present both sides of everything without actually answering the question?

Criterion Two: SEO Fluency Without Keyword Obsession

A QA content writer who understands search but cannot write for practitioners is a problem. So is one who can write for practitioners but has no concept of how buyers actually search for what they need. The right hire understands buyer search intent, knows how to structure content for featured snippets and AI-driven search results, and can weave keywords into natural prose without making the content feel like it was optimized rather than written.

As of 2026, this matters more than it did two years ago. AI-generated search overviews now pull from content that is structured clearly, answers questions directly, and demonstrates genuine expertise. Content that was keyword-stuffed or superficially researched is losing ground to content built on real authority. A QA content writer who understands this shift produces work that earns visibility in both traditional and AI-driven search.

Criterion Three: B2B Buyer Understanding

Writing that works for a QA engineer reading for learning is different from writing that works for a QA director evaluating a vendor or an engineering manager making a build versus buy decision. A qualified QA content writer understands these buyer distinctions and calibrates content accordingly. They know that decision-stage content needs to take clearer positions, use fewer qualifications, and make the business case alongside the technical one.

Ask any candidate you are evaluating to describe how they would approach an article targeting a QA director versus one targeting a QA engineer. The answer tells you a great deal about whether they think in terms of buyer psychology or just topic coverage.

Criterion Four: Long-Form Craft, Not Just Research Skills

Long-form content for a technical audience requires structural judgment that is separate from knowledge of the topic. A 2,000-word article about test automation strategy needs to open with a problem that the reader recognizes from experience, build an argument rather than a list, and reach a conclusion that earns the reader’s trust by the end. Many technically knowledgeable writers cannot do this. Many skilled writers cannot do it with technical content. The combination is genuinely rare.

What Are the Biggest Mistakes Testing Companies Make When They Hire a Content Writer?

The mistakes in this hiring process are predictable. They show up consistently across testing companies of different sizes and stages, and most of them happen before the first piece of content is ever published.

Mistake One: Treating QA Content Writing as a General Skill

The most expensive mistake is assuming that any competent content writer can cover software testing topics with enough briefing and research time. This assumption is wrong, and the evidence shows up in the content itself. Generalist writers produce content that looks like it should work. It has the right structure, the right keywords, and the right length. And then a QA professional reads it and immediately knows it was not written by someone who has done the work. That signal transfers to your brand and it is very hard to undo.

At QualiPulse, we have reviewed content programs from testing companies that were six months into a relationship with a general content agency. In every case, the articles had decent traffic and zero inbound attribution. The content was drawing awareness-stage readers, not decision-stage buyers, and it was not passing the practitioner test that would have kept the right readers engaged long enough to develop trust.

Mistake Two: Evaluating Writers on Portfolio Alone

Portfolio samples are a starting point, not a final evaluation. Content writing goes through editing, and a polished final piece often reflects as much about the editorial process as it does about the writer’s individual skill. The way to evaluate a QA content writer accurately is to give them a specific brief on a testing topic and evaluate the raw output before it goes through your review cycle. That reveals the actual baseline.

The brief should be specific enough to require practitioner knowledge. Ask for an article about the real cost of flaky tests in a continuous deployment environment, or a piece about what evaluation criteria actually matter when a team is choosing between testing frameworks for a complex microservices architecture. Generic prompts produce generic samples.

Mistake Three: Optimizing for Cost Over Quality

The cost of poor QA content is not what you pay the writer. It is the six months of consistent publishing that produced no qualified inbound leads, the brand association that your content created with an audience that was never going to buy from you, and the credibility deficit you created with practitioners who read your content and concluded that your company does not understand the work deeply enough to be trusted.

Content for a technical B2B audience in a specialized niche commands a premium for good reason. According to research from Draft.dev, companies in technical niches like developer tools should expect to pay significantly more per piece than general content rates, precisely because the combination of technical depth and writing quality is rare. The same logic applies when you hire a QA content writer. Optimizing for the cheapest option almost always produces the most expensive outcome.

Mistake Four: Skipping the Distribution Question

A QA content writer who only produces articles is half of what you need. Content that gets written, published on a blog, and shared once on LinkedIn on publication day compounds slowly. Content that gets written, distributed through email, reformatted for a newsletter, turned into LinkedIn posts by your leadership, and pushed into QA communities compounds much faster. Ask any writer candidate how they think about content distribution. The ones who only think about the article itself are not the right hire for a company trying to build a pipeline, not just traffic.

Freelancer, In-House, or Specialist Partner: Which Model Works for Testing Companies?

When you decide to hire a content writer for a testing company, the model matters as much as the individual. Each option has a different cost structure, quality profile, and operational requirement. Here is an honest breakdown.

Why Most Testing Companies End Up in the Freelancer Trap

Freelancer platforms are the default first move when a testing company decides to hire a content writer. The options look abundant, the cost looks manageable, and the process feels straightforward. The problem is that QA content writing is one of the hardest niches to hire for on a general freelancer platform because the credential signals are almost meaningless. A writer with five years of content experience and a sample article about test automation tells you very little about whether they can produce work that passes a QA practitioner’s scrutiny.

The typical pattern is: testing company posts a brief, receives several applications, hires based on portfolio and price, receives the first article, edits it heavily to fix technical inaccuracies, publishes it, and realizes six months later that the process is consuming more internal time than it is generating in pipeline value. The hidden cost of that cycle, the engineering or QA leader time spent reviewing for accuracy, the editorial rounds, the eventual realization that the content is not working, is usually far higher than the per-article rate suggested.

When In-House Makes Sense and When It Does Not

An in-house QA content writer makes sense when you have a sustained, high-volume need for content, internal editorial leadership to direct and develop the writer, and the runway to absorb a period of ramp-up before the writer produces work that consistently meets your quality bar. That combination exists in larger testing companies and well-funded QA tool vendors. It is rarely the right model for a mid-size testing consultancy or a growing automation tool company trying to build a content program from scratch.

The practical issue is that hiring a content writer who has both QA practitioner depth and professional writing skill is a long and difficult search. It is not impossible, but the pool is small, the compensation required to attract the right person is significant, and the management overhead of developing and retaining that person is a real operational commitment.

How Do You Run a Hiring Process That Actually Identifies the Right QA Content Writer?

Whether you are hiring a freelancer, an in-house writer, or evaluating a specialist content partner, the process should include the same core evaluation steps. Most companies skip too many of them and regret it.

Step One: Write a Brief That Requires Practitioner Knowledge

The quality of your brief determines the quality of the applicants you attract and the quality of the evaluation you can run. A brief that says write a 1500-word article about test automation for a QA audience will produce generic applications from generalist writers. A brief that says write a 1500-word article for QA directors evaluating whether their current automation coverage is ready to support a move to continuous deployment will filter out writers who cannot think from inside a practitioner’s decision context.

The topic you choose for a trial piece should be specific enough to require real knowledge and structured enough that you can evaluate the output against a clear standard. Give the same brief to two or three finalists and compare the results directly. The difference between practitioner-level output and researched output is usually obvious when you see them side by side.

Step Two: Ask the Right Questions in Evaluation

When evaluating candidates who want you to hire a QA content writer role with them, ask these directly.

  • Can you explain the difference between test coverage as a metric and test coverage as a risk management decision, without looking it up?
  • What does a QA director actually care about that a QA engineer does not, and how does that change how you write for each audience?
  • Give me an example of a testing topic where you would take a clear position rather than presenting both sides. What is the position and why?
  • How would you approach distributing a long-form article after it is published?
  • What does good look like for a piece of QA content in terms of conversion, not traffic?

The answers reveal whether the writer thinks in terms of buyer decisions or just topics, whether they understand the QA audience at a practitioner level, and whether they have a view on content performance that goes beyond page views.

Step Three: Pay for a Real Trial, Not a Spec Sample

The most reliable evaluation is a paid trial piece on a brief you would actually use. Pay the writer at their stated rate for a piece you can publish. This filters out writers who will not invest real effort in a trial, gives you output you can evaluate against real editorial standards, and creates a fair arrangement that attracts writers who take the work seriously.

Evaluate the trial piece on three dimensions. Technical accuracy, which means someone with QA delivery experience should read it and confirm it reflects how testing decisions actually work in practice. Writing quality, which means structure, flow, sentence clarity, and whether the argument builds coherently from introduction to conclusion. And buyer alignment, which means would a QA director reading this on a Thursday night before a vendor meeting find it useful or find it generic?

Why Working with a Specialist QA Content Partner Is Often the Better Alternative

The decision to hire a content writer as an individual versus working with a specialist content partner is ultimately a decision about where you want to carry the risk and overhead. Hiring an individual puts the risk on you: the search, the vetting, the ramp-up, the ongoing management, the quality review, and the strategic direction all require internal investment. Working with a specialist partner transfers that operational risk while giving you access to a model that has already solved the hardest part of the problem, which is combining practitioner depth with professional content production.

This is not an argument against hiring individual writers. It is an argument for being honest about what you are actually signing up for when you choose each path, and making the choice based on your actual internal capacity rather than the apparent simplicity of posting a job and hiring the best applicant.

What QualiPulse Offers Testing Companies That Need to Hire a QA Content Writer

The team has run enterprise QA programs, built automation frameworks, and navigated the specific organizational realities that QA buyers face. That experience goes into every piece of content produced, reviewed by QA professionals with real delivery experience, not just edited for grammar.

The QualiPulse Content Engine covers keyword research and topic planning based on buyer decision mapping, long-form articles reviewed by practitioners, infographics built for each piece, featured images, and distribution formats that convert each article into email-ready and newsletter-ready assets. Every deliverable is built to pass the practitioner test and the pipeline test. Frequently Asked Questions on How to Hire a QA Content Writer?

1. What does a QA content writer actually do?

A QA content writer produces marketing content specifically for the software testing industry. This includes long-form blog articles, whitepapers, guides, and thought leadership pieces that attract QA buyers through search, build brand authority in the testing space, and support pipeline generation. Unlike a technical writer who produces documentation, a QA content writer focuses on content that earns search rankings, builds trust with a practitioner audience, and contributes to inbound lead generation over time. The role requires both genuine testing knowledge and professional-grade writing skill.

2. Why is it hard to hire a QA content writer with expertise?

The combination of practitioner-level testing knowledge and professional content writing skill is genuinely rare. Most writers who understand QA do not have the content marketing fluency to produce work that ranks, converts, and holds up structurally across long-form formats. Most professional content writers can research testing topics well enough to produce plausible-sounding articles, but those articles fail the practitioner test that QA buyers apply almost automatically. Finding someone who holds both skills at a high enough level for a demanding technical audience is the core difficulty.

3. What should a QA content writer’s trial piece look like?

A good trial piece for evaluating a QA content writer should address a specific decision that a QA buyer faces, not a general educational topic. It should be 1,500 to 2,000 words, structured as an argument rather than a listicle, and include enough technical specificity that a working QA engineer would confirm it reflects real practitioner thinking. Evaluate the output on three dimensions: technical accuracy confirmed by a QA professional on your team, writing quality, including structure and flow, and buyer alignment, meaning whether a decision-stage buyer would find it genuinely useful.

4. How much should I expect to pay to hire a QA content writer?

Rates for specialist technical content in B2B niches vary significantly based on the model. For freelancers with genuine QA depth and professional writing skill, expect to pay considerably more than general content rates because the combination is uncommon. Published research from technical content providers suggests developer tool and technical niche content can run between 1,200 and 1,800 USD per piece at the high end for strong independent writers. Agency and specialist partner models typically offer more predictable monthly pricing that includes strategy, writing, review, and distribution formats.

5. What is the difference between a QA content writer and a technical writer?

A technical writer produces documentation: user manuals, API references, product guides, and internal process documentation. A QA content writer produces marketing content designed to attract buyers, rank in search, and build brand authority. The audiences, goals, and success metrics are completely different. A technical writer succeeds when a user can follow the documentation to complete a task. A QA content writer succeeds when a QA director reads an article and reaches out to start a conversation with the company that published it. Both roles require technical knowledge, but they serve entirely different purposes.

6. Should I hire a content writer in-house or work with a specialist content partner?

In-house hiring makes sense if you have consistently high content volume requirements, internal editorial leadership to direct and develop the writer, and the runway to absorb a ramp-up period before the writer reaches full productivity. For most mid-size testing companies and growing QA tool vendors, the specialist partner model delivers better outcomes with less internal overhead because the vetting, practitioner review, strategy, and distribution are already built into the engagement. The right answer depends on your content volume, internal capacity, and how quickly you need results.

7. How do I know if a QA content writer sample is actually good?

Show the sample to a working QA engineer or test lead on your team without identifying the author. Ask them whether it reads like it was written by someone who has done the work or by someone who researched the topic. That single test is more reliable than any portfolio credential or agency pitch. Specific signals of genuine quality include: the writer takes clear positions on contested testing questions rather than presenting both sides without answering anything, the technical examples reflect real practitioner situations rather than textbook scenarios, and the business case is made alongside the technical argument rather than treating them as separate concerns.

You can request a sample to see the difference practitioner-led content makes before committing. Visit qualipulse.tech to learn more.

Conclusion

The decision to hire a QA content writer is easy to make and hard to execute well. The combination of genuine testing practitioner knowledge and professional content writing skill is rare enough that most testing companies either settle for the wrong hire or discover the problem six months and several published articles too late.

The right approach starts with clarity about what you actually need: not a generalist who can research testing topics, but someone who can write with the authority of a practitioner and the structure of a professional content strategist. Whether that is a skilled individual writer, an in-house hire, or a specialist partner, the hiring criteria and the evaluation process are the same. Pass the practitioner test first. Everything else follows from there.
